# ISLAM v. ATTORNEY GENERAL UNITED STATES OF AMERICA (2026)
## United States Court of Appeals, Third Circuit.
### No. 25-1101

### Decided: October 14, 2026

### Before: Krause, Phipps, and Chung, Circuit Judges
## United States Court of Appeals, Third Circuit.
Sofiqul Islam invites us to disregard our prior interpretation of the phrase “sexual abuse of a minor” in the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(43)(A), in view of the Supreme Court's decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 144 S.Ct. 2244,
Our precedent controls here and forecloses Islam's arguments that the New York statute under which he was convicted for second-degree sexual abuse criminalizes a broader range of conduct than the federal generic offense of sexual abuse of a minor. For that reason, and because Islam's other claims of error are unavailing, we will dismiss in part and deny in part his petition for review.
Yet by 2009, Islam nevertheless decided that he “could no longer live a normal life in Bangladesh as an active BNP member.” A.R. 227 ¶ 6. He then immigrated to New York to join his wife, a U.S. citizen whom he had married in 2006 and with whom he has two children who are also U.S. citizens.
B. Islam's Conviction and Removal Proceedings

In May 2022, Islam was arrested and pleaded guilty to one count of misdemeanor sexual abuse in the second degree under New York Penal Law (NYPL) § 130.60(2), which prohibits “sexual contact” with a person “[l]ess than fourteen years old.” Islam was sentenced to 364 days in jail. This was his first arrest and criminal charge.
At the conclusion of his sentence, the Department of Homeland Security apprehended Islam and served him with a Notice to Appear, which, as relevant here, charged him as removable on the basis that his New York conviction constituted an aggravated felony under the INA—specifically, the sexual abuse of a minor predicate offense. ### Comparing offenses, not reconstructing events

The court used the categorical approach described in Moncrieffe v. Holder, 569 U.S. 184 (2013), and Shular v. United States, 589 U.S. 154 (2020). It first identified the federal generic offense and then compared that definition with the elements necessary for conviction under New York law.

Mathis v. United States, 579 U.S. 500 (2016), supplied the central instruction: disregard the particular facts of the defendant’s conduct and compare the legal elements. Thus, the inquiry was not what Islam actually did, but whether the New York provision criminalized conduct outside the federal category.

New York’s misdemeanor classification and Islam’s sentence did not resolve that inquiry. “Aggravated felony” is a federal statutory designation; the sexual-abuse-of-a-minor category does not depend on whether state law labels the offense a felony.

Sofiqul ISLAM, Petitioner v. ATTORNEY GENERAL UNITED STATES OF AMERICA

Opinion of the Court
Sofiqul Islam invites us to disregard our prior interpretation of the phrase “sexual abuse of a minor” in the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(43)(A), in view of the Supreme Court's decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Our precedent controls here and forecloses Islam's arguments that the New York statute under which he was convicted for second-degree sexual abuse criminalizes a broader range of conduct than the federal generic offense of sexual abuse of a minor. For that reason, and because Islam's other claims of error are unavailing, we will dismiss in part and deny in part his petition for review.

In sum, there is no categorical mismatch between the mens rea of the federal generic definition of sexual abuse of a minor and Islam's statute of conviction: The proscribed touching in both must be knowing or intentional. Accord Garcia Pinach, 147 F.4th at 130 (concluding that the mens rea of NYPL § 130.60(2) is not overbroad as compared to the federal generic definition of sexual abuse of a minor).

## United States Court of Appeals, Third Circuit.
###
Sofiqul ISLAM, Petitioner v. ATTORNEY GENERAL UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
### No. 25-1101
### Decided: October 14, 2026

Opinion of the Court
Sofiqul Islam invites us to disregard our prior interpretation of the phrase “sexual abuse of a minor” in the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(43)(A), in view of the Supreme Court's decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 144 S.Ct. 2244, 219 L.Ed.2d 832 (2024). We decline. The full implications of Loper Bright on our Court's interpretation of federal statutes have yet to be determined, but one thing is already clear: While Loper Bright has prohibited us from applying Chevron deference to agencies' interpretations of ambiguous statutory provisions going forward, see Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837, 104 S.Ct. 2778, 81 L.Ed.2d 694 (1984), it also sought to minimize disruption to existing precedent which already applied that deference. Our precedent controls here and forecloses Islam's arguments that the New York statute under which he was convicted for second-degree sexual abuse criminalizes a broader range of conduct than the federal generic offense of sexual abuse of a minor. For that reason, and because Islam's other claims of error are unavailing, we will dismiss in part and deny in part his petition for review.

In sum, there is no categorical mismatch between the mens rea of the federal generic definition of sexual abuse of a minor and Islam's statute of conviction: The proscribed touching in both must be knowing or intentional. Accord Garcia Pinach, 147 F.4th at 130 (concluding that the mens rea of NYPL § 130.60(2) is not overbroad as compared to the federal generic definition of sexual abuse of a minor).

For the foregoing reasons, we will dismiss Islam's petition for review as to his removability and deny it as to his CAT claim.

## United States Court of Appeals, Third Circuit.
###
Sofiqul ISLAM, Petitioner v. ATTORNEY GENERAL UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
### No. 25-1101
### Decided: October 14, 2026

Opinion of the Court
Sofiqul Islam invites us to disregard our prior interpretation of the phrase “sexual abuse of a minor” in the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(43)(A), in view of the Supreme Court's decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 144 S.Ct. 2244, 219 L.Ed.2d 832 (2024). We decline. The full implications of Loper Bright on our Court's interpretation of federal statutes have yet to be determined, but one thing is already clear: While Loper Bright has prohibited us from applying Chevron deference to agencies' interpretations of ambiguous statutory provisions going forward, see Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837, 104 S.Ct. 2778, 81 L.Ed.2d 694 (1984), it also sought to minimize disruption to existing precedent which already applied that deference. Our precedent controls here and forecloses Islam's arguments that the New York statute under which he was convicted for second-degree sexual abuse criminalizes a broader range of conduct than the federal generic offense of sexual abuse of a minor. For that reason, and because Islam's other claims of error are unavailing, we will dismiss in part and deny in part his petition for review.

In sum, there is no categorical mismatch between the mens rea of the federal generic definition of sexual abuse of a minor and Islam's statute of conviction: The proscribed touching in both must be knowing or intentional. Accord Garcia Pinach, 147 F.4th at 130 (concluding that the mens rea of NYPL § 130.60(2) is not overbroad as compared to the federal generic definition of sexual abuse of a minor).

For the foregoing reasons, we will dismiss Islam's petition for review as to his removability and deny it as to his CAT claim.
